```{r message = F}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)
```

# Problem 1 

## Data import
```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)

data("ny_noaa")
```

This dataset has `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns and `r nrow(ny_noaa)` rows. It has a number of variables to show weather data from around the world. These variables include the weather station `id`, the `date` when the measurements were taken, and the measurements themselves, including precipitation `prcp`, amount of snow `snow`, snow depth `snwd`, and maximum `tmax` and minimum `tmin` temperatures. Missing data seems to be a significant issue in this dataset, as many of the data is `NA`. 

## Data Cleaning 

```{r}
noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>  
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date), 
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date), 
    prcp = as.numeric(prcp), 
    snow = as.numeric(snow),
    snwd = as.numeric(snwd), 
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax),
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin), 
    tmax = tmax / 10, 
    tmin = tmin / 10, 
    prcp = prcp / 10
    ) 
```

## Most commonly observed snowfall

```{r}
noaa_df |> 
  group_by(snow) |> 
  summarise(
    n_snow = n()
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(n_snow)) |> 
  head(10) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The most commonly observed value of snow is 0mm. This makes sense, as snow does not fall most of the time. 

## Average tmax across years in January and July 

```{r}
noaa_df |>
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |> 
  group_by(year, month) |> 
  summarize(
    avg_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = avg_tmax)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_grid(.~ month) +
  theme_minimal()  +
   labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July Across Years",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature"
  )
```
This plot shows a clear distinction between the average maximum temperatures in January compared to July across years. July temperatures seem to have remained relatively steady between 1980 and 2010, but January temperatures show a sharp increase in the 1980s before plateauing.  

## Two panel plot

```{r}
tmax_v_tmin_plot = 
  noaa_df |>  
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) + 
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Minimum temp vs. maximum temp across all stations",
    x = "Minimum temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (C)"
  )

snow_plot = 
  noaa_df |> 
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> 
  mutate(
    year = factor(year)
    ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) + 
  geom_density_ridges() +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall distributions across years"
  )

tmax_v_tmin_plot / snow_plot
```

# Problem 2

## Import, clean, and tidy the data 

```{r}
demographic_df =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_demographics.csv",
           skip = 4,
           na = c("", "NA", ".")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex, 
     1 ~ c("male"), 
     2 ~ c("female")), 
    education = case_match(
      education, 
      1 ~ c("less than high school"), 
      2 ~ c("high school equivalent"), 
      3 ~ c("more than high school")
    ))
```

```{r}
accelerometer_df = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv", 
           na = c("", "NA", ".")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440, 
    names_to = "minute", 
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  )
```

## Merge the datasets 

```{r}
demo_accel_df = 
  left_join(demographic_df, accelerometer_df, by = "seqn")
```

## Making a reader-friendly table  

```{r}
demo_accel_df |> 
  group_by(education, sex) |> 
  summarize(
    n_people = n_distinct(seqn)
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
There are a similar number of men and women who have more than a high school education, and a similar number of men and women who have less than a high school education. Interestingly, many more men have a high school equivalent education compared to women. More people have more than a high school education compared to any other education category. 

## Making a visualization 

```{r}
demo_accel_df |> 
  mutate(education = fct_relevel(education, c("less than high school", "high school equivalent", "more than high school"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution for men and women in each educational category"
  ) +
  viridis::scale_color_viridis(
    discrete = TRUE
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Both men and women who completed more than a high school education tend to be younger than the compare groups, and both men and women who who completed less than a high school education tend to be older than the compare groups. Interestingly, of those who completed only a high school equivalent of education, the women tend to be older and the men tend to be younger. 

## Total activity 

```{r}
demo_accel_df |>  
  group_by(seqn) |> 
  mutate(
    activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  theme_minimal()
```
This plot shows general downward trends in activity levels across education levels and sexes. However, there are large variations in activity levels within each of these groups. Participants with more than a high school education tend to have less change in activity level as they age, although there is still a slight downward trend. 

## Activity over the day 

```{r}
demo_accel_df |> 
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute)
  ) |> 
  group_by(minute, education, sex) |>
  summarize( 
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute / 60, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line() + 
  geom_smooth() +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 6)) +
  labs(
    title = "24-hour activity time courses across  education level and sex",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Mean MIMS"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
This plot shows the activity levels of participants over the course of 24 hours, across each education level and sex. In general, women tend to have higher activity levels than men. Those with less than a high school education have higher activity level peaks earlier in the day than those with more than a high school education or with a high school education equivalent. However, those with more than a high school education have more sustained activity throughout the day than other education levels. 

# Problem 3 

## Import and clean data 

```{r}
jan2020_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv", 
           na = c("", "NA", ".")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month = "jan", 
         year = "2020") 
```

```{r}
jan2024_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv", 
           na = c("", "NA", ".")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names()|> 
  mutate(month = "jan", 
         year = "2024") 
```

```{r}
july2020_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv", 
           na = c("", "NA", ".")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month = "july",
         year = "2020") 
```

```{r}
july2024_df = 
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv", 
           na = c("", "NA", ".")) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month = "july", 
         year = "2024") 
```

# Do i need to tidy more?

## Binding Rows 

```{r}
citi_bikes_df = 
  bind_rows(jan2020_df, july2020_df, jan2024_df, july2024_df) |> 
  relocate(month, year) |> 
  drop_na()
```

## Table 1 

```{r}
citi_bikes_df |> 
  group_by(month, year, member_casual) |> 
  summarize(
    rides = n()
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
This table shows that the total number of rides occurring increased over 4 years, at least doubling in most cases, showing an increase in popularity of Citi Bikes. In both 2020 and 2024, there were more riders of all types in the summer, but casual riders specifically significantly increased.

## Most popular starting stations

```{r}
citi_bikes_df |> 
  filter(month == "july", year == "2024") |> 
  group_by(start_station_name) |> 
  summarize(
    rides = n()) |> 
  arrange(desc(rides)) |> 
  slice_head(n = 5) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
In July 2024, the most popular start station was Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers, with 163 total rides occurring. 

## Plot of effect of weekday, month, and year on median ride duration 

```{r}
citi_bikes_df |> 
  group_by(weekdays, month, year) |> 
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = month, group = month)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line () +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)) +
  facet_grid(. ~year) +
   labs(
    title = "Median ride duration across different weekdays, months, and years",
    y = "median ride duration"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"))
```
Interestingly, the median ride duration decreased in both January and July from 2020 to 2024. This may be a result of increasing prices for longer Citi Bike rides. In July, ride duration tends to be longer, most likely due to the warmer weather. For both January and July in 2020 and 2024, the longest median ride duration occurs on Saturday. The weekend tends to have longer ride duration, except for Sunday in January 2024, which has significantly shorter ride durations. 

## Plot of the impact of month, membership status, and bike type of ride duration

```{r}
citi_bikes_df |> 
  filter(year == "2024", duration > 0) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = rideable_type, y = duration, fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_grid(.~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "The impact of month, membership status, and bike type of ride duration",
    x = "bike type",
    y = "ride duration (log scale)",
    fill = "membership status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
There were many ride duration data point outliers in this data set, most likely due to improper docking. These dramatically skewed the plot. In order to better interpret the data, I changed the ride duration to a log scale. For Citi Bike members, bike type and month do not have huge impacts on ride duration. This may be because members tend to use Citi Bikes more regularly, for purposes like commuting, which has a similar duration year round. However, for casual riders, ride duration is longer on classic bikes, which are less expensive than electric bikes, and in July, which is better weather for biking than January.
